result: Human chemically induced liver progenitors (hCLiPs) can be generated from infant primary human hepatocytes (IPHHs) using small molecule inhibitors (A83-01 and CHIR99021) combined with FBS. These hCLiPs exhibit significant repopulative capacity in injured mouse livers, can redifferentiate into mature hepatocytes in vitro, and display CYP enzymatic activities comparable to primary human hepatocytes.
evaluation: Claims C4-C8 collectively describe the main findings of the study. The generation of hCLiPs from IPHHs (C4) is supported by extensive experimental data including morphological observations, marker expression, and transcriptomic analysis. The repopulative capacity (C5) is demonstrated through transplantation experiments showing RIs >90% in some animals. Redifferentiation capacity (C6) and CYP activities (C7, C8) are supported by gene expression, enzymatic assays, and protein quantification data across multiple donor-derived cell lines.

result: Culture of IPHHs in medium containing A83-01, CHIR99021, and FBS (FAC) induces proliferation of hepatic epithelial cells with progenitor-like characteristics. These cells spontaneously acquire hepatocyte-like morphology when densely packed and proliferate more efficiently than adult PHHs (APHHs), with fold expansion varying among donor lots (3.66-49.2 fold at day 12-14).
evaluation: Claims C17-C31 describe the initial characterization of hCLiP induction from IPHHs. The proliferation in FAC is supported by WST assays (C25, C26), morphological observations (C17, C18, C28), and quantitative measurements of fold expansion (C30). The synergistic effect of AC and FBS (C27) is demonstrated experimentally. The superior proliferation of IPHHs compared to APHHs (C29) is consistently observed across multiple experiments and donor lots (C30, C31).

result: Proliferating cells cultured in FAC express multiple liver progenitor cell (LPC) surface markers (EPCAM, CD44, PROM1, CD24, ITGA6) and upregulate BEC/LPC marker genes (EPCAM, SOX9, KRT19, TACSTD2, AXIN2, PROX1) while maintaining hepatocytic characteristics, as demonstrated by enrichment of hepatic function-related gene sets.
evaluation: Claims C32-C41 characterize the molecular phenotype of hCLiPs. Flow cytometry data (C32, Figure 2D) demonstrates surface marker expression, with appropriate controls showing minimal expression in PHHs before culture (C33, C34). Microarray analysis (C35-C38, Figure 2E-F) confirms upregulation of BEC/LPC genes with statistical analysis. GSEA results (C39, C40, Figure 2G) support maintenance of hepatic characteristics. The data collectively support a hybrid hepatocyte/LPC phenotype.

result: IPHHs are more responsive to AC treatment than APHHs, as evidenced by distinct transcriptomic clustering and differential pathway enrichment. IPHHs show enriched Wnt signaling (nominal p=0.019) and higher expression of LPC-related Wnt target genes (AXIN2, LGR5), while both cell types respond to TGFβ inhibition. The lower proliferative capacity of APHHs may be partly explained by their reduced responsiveness to Wnt signaling.
evaluation: Claims C42-C58 compare IPHHs and APHHs responses to FAC treatment. Hierarchical clustering (C42, C43, Figure 3A) clearly separates IPHHs but not APHHs cultured in FAC from FBS controls. GSEA data (C48, C50) with reported p-values support differential pathway enrichment. Gene expression analysis (C51-C54, Figure 3C-D) confirms both cell types respond to individual pathway components but differ in LPC-related gene expression. The inference about proliferative capacity (C58) is reasonable but acknowledged as requiring further analysis.

result: hCLiPs can redifferentiate into mature hepatocyte-like cells upon treatment with hepatic maturation inducers (OSM, dexamethasone, Matrigel). Redifferentiated cells (Hep-i(+)) acquire hepatocyte morphology, upregulate hepatic marker genes (ALB, TDO2, SERPINA1), downregulate BEC/LPC markers (SOX9, KRT19, KRT7), and exhibit transcriptomic profiles similar to primary hepatocytes with enrichment of immune response and metabolic pathways.
evaluation: Claims C59-C70 describe hepatic differentiation capacity of hCLiPs. Morphological changes (C59-C61) are documented with microscopy (Figure 4A-B). Gene expression changes (C62-C64) are supported by microarray data (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). Hierarchical clustering (C65, Figure 4D) demonstrates similarity to PHHs. Pathway analysis (C66-C69, Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D) supports functional maturation with appropriate statistical analysis. The data collectively demonstrate differentiation capacity.

result: Redifferentiated hCLiPs (Hep-i(+)) express major drug-metabolizing CYP genes (CYP2B6, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, CYP2C9, CYP3A4) and exhibit basal CYP enzymatic activities comparable to PHHs (for lots FCL and JFC). CYP activities are inducible by specific inducers (omeprazole, phenobarbital, rifampicin), with greater induction in Hep-i(+) than Hep-i(-) cells. Phase II enzyme (SULT, UGT) activities are also comparable to PHHs.
evaluation: Claims C71-C80 characterize drug metabolism capacity. Microarray data (C71, C72, Figure 5A) shows CYP gene expression. LC-MS/MS measurements (C73, C74, Figure 5B) quantify basal enzymatic activities with appropriate comparisons to PHHs, noting lot-specific variation. CYP induction (C75-C77, Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) is demonstrated at both gene and protein levels (C78, Figure 5D). Phase II enzyme activities (C79, Figure 5E) complete the metabolic characterization. The data support potential application in drug metabolism studies (C80).

result: hCLiPs can be serially passaged until at least P10 with population doubling times of 1.27-1.43 days, maintain diploid karyotype, but gradually lose hepatic phenotype during extended culture. Despite functional decline, hCLiPs at P3 and P5 retain capacity for hepatic differentiation and CYP3A induction, though basal CYP activities decrease with passage number. Contamination with fibroblast-like cells varies among donor lots.
evaluation: Claims C81-C99 characterize long-term culture properties. Growth curves (C81, C82, Figure 6A) document serial passage capacity with quantified doubling times. Karyotyping (C87, Figure 6B) confirms genetic stability. Transcriptomic analysis (C89-C91, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) and qRT-PCR (C92, Figure 6C) demonstrate gradual phenotypic changes. Functional assays (C93-C97, Figure 6C-E) show maintained differentiation capacity and CYP3A induction despite declining basal activities. The presence of contaminating cells (C83-C86) is documented but does not invalidate the main findings about hCLiP properties.

result: Enrichment of LPC marker-positive cells (EPCAM+, PROM1+, CD24+) from hCLiP cultures yields cells with hepatic phenotype, while THY1+ cells exhibit mesenchymal characteristics. However, even after enrichment, LPC marker+ cells show reduced LPC/hepatic phenotypes after three passages compared to P0, indicating that phenotypic deterioration is unavoidable.
evaluation: Claims C100-C104 describe cell sorting experiments to address heterogeneity. qRT-PCR data (C100, C101, Figure 7B) clearly distinguishes LPC marker+ cells (expressing ALB, TTR, GJB1) from THY1+ cells (expressing ACTA2, VIM). Follow-up analysis (C102, Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) shows relative retention of phenotype compared to THY1+ cells. However, comparison to P0 (C103, Figure 7—figure supplement 2) demonstrates substantial phenotypic loss, supporting the conclusion that deterioration is unavoidable (C104). The data are internally consistent.

result: P0-hCLiPs demonstrate significant repopulative capacity in cDNA-uPA/SCID mice, with maximum hALB levels >10 mg/ml and RIs reaching >90% in some animals (mean RIs: 32.2±13.5% for FCL, 39.3±13.5% for JFC, 17.8±16.4% for DUX). This maximum RI is comparable to PHHs and to ProliHH cells. Repopulative capacity declines with passage number, though some P1 and P2 cells (after ~400-1000-fold expansion) still achieve high RIs (67-91%).
evaluation: Claims C105-C118 describe transplantation results in cDNA-uPA/SCID mice. Blood hALB measurements (C105, C106, Figure 8A) and IHC quantification (C107-C109, Figure 8B-C) provide convergent evidence for repopulation. Statistical data with SEMs (C108) show variability but substantial mean RIs. Comparisons to PHHs (C110) and ProliHH (C117, C118) are appropriately cited. Decline with passage (C111) is demonstrated, but notable exceptions (C112, C113) with high RIs after substantial expansion (C114, C115) are documented. The dichotomous response pattern is acknowledged but does not invalidate the positive results.

result: In TK-NOG mice, FCL-P0-hCLiPs achieve maximum serum hALB of 8.1 mg/ml and maximum RI of 57.5%, lower than in cDNA-uPA/SCID mice (96.0%), but with more efficient engraftment (83% vs 50% with >15% RI). Repopulating cells express hepatic function markers (MDR1, TTR), reconstruct normal liver architecture with proper apical-basolateral polarity, and establish correct hepatic zonation (GLUL, CYP1A2, CYP3A4).
evaluation: Claims C119-C125 describe transplantation in an alternative mouse model. Quantitative measurements (C119, C120, Figure 8D-F) show lower maximum RI but improved engraftment efficiency (C121), suggesting model-specific differences. IHC data (C122-C125, Figure 8G-I) demonstrate functional integration with proper expression of hepatic markers, correct cellular polarity (C123), and appropriate zonation patterns (C124, C125). The data support functional maturation in vivo despite lower maximum RI than cDNA-uPA/SCID model.

result: hCLiPs at later passages (P3-P4) show dramatically reduced repopulative capacity. FCL-P4-hCLiPs produce hALB levels ~1/1000 of high-RI mice and achieve RIs <1%. FCL-P3-hCLiPs with hepatic induction (Hep-i(+)) show higher hALB than uninduced cells but still only 9.1±1.8 μg/ml at 8 weeks. These results demonstrate that extended in vitro culture unavoidably decreases repopulative capacity.
evaluation: Claims C126-C131 document loss of repopulative capacity with extended culture. Quantitative hALB measurements (C126, C127, C130, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, 1C) show dramatic decreases compared to P0-P1 cells. IHC quantification (C128, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) confirms very low RIs. The comparison between Hep-i(+) and Hep-i(-) P3 cells (C129) shows hepatic induction provides some benefit but insufficient for substantial repopulation. The conclusion (C131) is well-supported by the data, though the underlying mechanisms are not fully elucidated.

result: hCLiP-derived hepatocytes isolated from chimeric mouse livers exhibit mature hepatocyte morphology and functional maturation. Despite transcriptomic differences from PHHs (likely due to mouse liver environment), these cells show enrichment of hepatic function-related gene sets (especially metabolic pathways), downregulation of BEC/LPC markers, basal CYP activities comparable to PHHs, robust CYP induction by specific inducers, and comparable phase II enzyme activities.
evaluation: Claims C132-C145 characterize hCLiPs after in vivo maturation. Morphological observations (C132, Figure 9A) and transcriptomic analysis (C133-C135, Figure 9B-C) show differences from PHHs, but the control experiment with transplanted IPHHs (C134) appropriately attributes this to environmental factors rather than incomplete maturation. GSEA (C136-C138, Figure 9D) demonstrates enrichment of hepatic functions. Downregulation of LPC markers (C139, C140) supports maturation. Functional assays (C141-C144, Figure 9E-G) demonstrate comparable metabolic capacity to PHHs. The conclusion (C145) appropriately acknowledges transcriptomic differences while emphasizing functional maturation.

result: A mini-screen of small molecules Y (Y-27632), A (A83-01), and C (CHIR99021) demonstrates that A and C individually accelerate PHH proliferation while Y shows no beneficial effect and even negatively affects proliferation when combined with AC. This synergistic effect of A83-01 and CHIR99021 is consistent with previous observations in rodent hepatocytes and represents the key mechanism for hepatocyte proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C163-C167 describe mechanistic insights from the mini-screen. The experimental data (C163, C164, Figure 2A) clearly show differential effects of small molecule combinations. Comparison with previous rodent work (C165, C166) provides cross-species validation. The conclusion about synergistic effects (C167) is well-supported by the data, though the molecular mechanisms underlying the synergy are not fully elucidated in this study.

result: Comparative analysis suggests that Wnt signaling activity in response to CHIR99021 may partly explain the proliferative ability of IPHHs, while APHHs respond equally or more efficiently to A83-01. Since A83-01 is essential for IPHH proliferation, it might affect IPHHs through a TGFβ-independent mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C168-C171 propose mechanistic explanations for differential proliferation. The inference about Wnt signaling (C168) is supported by GSEA data (C48) but acknowledged as partial explanation. The observation about A83-01 response (C169) is supported by gene expression data (C53, C54). However, the speculation about TGFβ-independent mechanisms (C171) is not directly tested. The claims represent reasonable hypotheses requiring further investigation, as acknowledged by the authors. Additional experiments (e.g., testing alternative TGFβ inhibitors, Wnt pathway manipulation) would be needed to definitively support these mechanistic claims.

result: The study addresses a significant unmet need in liver regenerative medicine. Hepatocytes are the only effective cell source for transplantation but are limited by donor shortage and inability to proliferate in vitro. Laboratory-generated hepatocytes have poor repopulative capacity (typically <5% RI), though recent studies including Zhang et al. (2018) reported higher RIs (up to 64%). The current work contributes to this emerging field of generating proliferative hepatic cells from PHHs.
evaluation: Claims C1-C153 establish the context and significance of the work. The statements about hepatocytes as the only effective cell source (C1, C9), limitations (C2, C10, C13, C14), and poor performance of laboratory-generated cells (C11, C12, C148) are appropriately cited and represent established knowledge. The comparison with recent work (C149-C153) appropriately acknowledges concurrent developments in the field, particularly the Zhang et al. study with similar high RIs. The authors appropriately position their work as contributing independent validation to an emerging concept.

result: hCLiPs represent a novel platform for drug discovery studies. CYP inducibility is the major criterion for drug metabolism studies, as CYP enzymes play central roles in drug metabolism and CYP induction affects xenobiotic clearance. While PHHs lose CYP inducibility in culture and laboratory-generated hepatocytes show limited CYP induction, hCLiPs demonstrate robust CYP induction at the enzymatic activity level.
evaluation: Claims C154-C162 propose hCLiPs as a drug discovery platform. The importance of CYP inducibility (C155-C158) is established knowledge appropriately cited. The limitations of existing systems (C159-C161) are well-documented in the literature. The experimental data (C71-C80) demonstrating CYP induction in hCLiPs support the proposal (C154, C162). However, this represents a potential application rather than a fully validated platform—additional studies comparing hCLiPs to PHHs in actual drug screening scenarios would strengthen this claim.

result: Comparison with recent literature reveals important differences in culture conditions and mechanisms. HGF is used in all four recent PHH expansion studies and may play a critical role, particularly emphasized by Kim et al. (2019) in the presence of AC. Zhang et al. (2018) attribute proliferation to Wnt3a (not substitutable by CHIR99021 or Rspo1) and propose hypoxic culture suppresses senescence. Fu et al. showed nicotinamide (a sirtuin suppressor) decreases PHH proliferation, highlighting human-rodent differences since nicotinamide induces rat hepatocyte proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C172-C180 provide important context by comparing the current work with concurrent studies. The observations about HGF (C172-C174), Wnt signaling mechanisms (C175, C176), hypoxia (C177), and nicotinamide effects (C178-C180) are appropriately cited and accurately represent the referenced studies. These comparisons highlight both similarities and differences in approaches, suggesting multiple pathways may contribute to PHH expansion. The discussion appropriately acknowledges that the current study does not include HGF or hypoxia, representing areas for future optimization.
